title: Perspective on Tax Cost | Dimensional
gist: Dimensional argues that expense ratios understate the true cost of fund ownership because tax cost ratios—the share of pre-tax return lost to taxes—can be roughly twice a fund's expense ratio, with nonqualified dividend income (notably from REITs) the leak an ETF wrapper cannot plug. The piece is a short two-minute perspective anchored on a Morningstar category exhibit as of December 31, 2025; the exhibit's underlying numbers are not reproduced in the text, so only the 'twice as big' magnitude is stated.

themes.theme: Expense ratio as an incomplete cost metric

insights.claim: Comparing expense ratios between mutual funds and ETFs fails to capture the total cost of ownership of a fund, and tax cost is among the largest omitted line items.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Screen funds on after-tax total cost of ownership rather than headline fee; cheapest-by-expense-ratio screens can systematically pick the wrong vehicle in taxable accounts.
insights.quote: Investors spend a lot of time comparing expense ratios between mutual funds and ETFs. While these are important characteristics, they fall short in capturing the total cost of ownership for investments.

insights.claim: Morningstar category tax cost ratios—the percent of pre-tax return lost after taxes—can be twice as large as a fund's net expense ratio, measured as of December 31, 2025.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: A 2x multiplier on fee drag means tax efficiency, not fee compression, is the larger remaining lever on net returns for taxable investors.

insights.claim: A low headline expense ratio can be misleading because the tax bill on distributions arrives separately and can dominate the fee saving.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Use all-in cost (expense ratio + tax cost ratio) as the comparison unit when ranking otherwise similar funds.
insights.quote: A fund with a low expense ratio might not seem so cheap once the tax bill comes due.

themes.theme: Limits of the ETF wrapper on income

insights.claim: The ETF structure can defer realized capital gains but does not shield investors from distributed income, so the wrapper's tax advantage is partial rather than general.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Do not assume an ETF conversion or ETF share class solves tax drag for income-heavy strategies; the benefit concentrates in gains-driven, low-yield exposures.
insights.quote: While ETFs may enable investors to delay realizing gains, income may be a different story, especially if the fund holds securities that distribute nonqualified dividend income, such as REITs.

insights.claim: Funds holding securities that distribute nonqualified dividend income, such as REITs, are singled out as the case where tax cost is most likely to swamp the fee advantage.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Flags REIT and other high-nonqualified-income sleeves as candidates to move into tax-deferred accounts rather than taxable ETF holdings.
insights.locator: While ETFs may enable investors to delay

insights.claim: Fund-level tax cost arises from two distinct channels—capital gains distributed when the fund sells a security at a profit, and dividend income paid out by portfolio companies—which respond to different portfolio design choices.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: Separates turnover-driven tax drag (addressable by wrapper and trading design) from yield-driven drag (addressable only by asset location or security selection).
insights.quote: Taxes can be incurred through a combination of capital gains and dividend income.

insights.claim: Qualified dividend income is taxed at the lower capital gains rates while nonqualified income is taxed at the higher ordinary income rate, making the qualified/nonqualified split a direct driver of a fund's after-tax return.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: The qualified share of a fund's distributions is a screenable variable that materially changes realized after-tax yield between otherwise identical funds.
insights.quote: Qualified dividend income is taxed at lower capital gains tax rates, while nonqualified income is taxed at the higher ordinary income rate.

insights.claim: REITs are structurally forced to distribute nearly all of their earnings to shareholders, which is the mechanism that makes their income stream persistently tax-inefficient rather than a temporary condition.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: REIT tax drag cannot be engineered away at the fund level, so asset location is the only real lever for taxable investors seeking real-asset income exposure.
insights.quote: REITs must hold most of their assets in real estate, derive most of their revenue from real estate related sources, and distribute nearly all of their earnings to shareholders.
